title: 1 Samuel 21:1–9
context: Having said goodbye to Jonathan, David flees from Saul with nothing. At Nob, the town of the priests, he tells Ahimelech a false story about a secret mission, receives the holy bread that had been removed from before the LORD, and takes Goliath's sword. A silent witness, Doeg the Edomite, sees it all, which sets up the tragedy of chapter 22. Jesus later cites this episode in the Gospels (Matthew 12:3–4; Mark 2:25–26).

verses.text: Then David came to Nob to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech came to meet David trembling, and said to him, “Why are you alone, and no man with you?”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimelech meets David "trembling," sensing something is wrong. Arminian readers note that the anointed future king arrives alone and vulnerable, a man who must now walk by trust in God rather than royal favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's chosen king is a fugitive, the promise apparently far from fulfillment. Mark 2:26 speaks of "the time of Abiathar the high priest," a well-known difficulty interpreters resolve in various ways.

verses.text: David said to Ahimelech the priest, “The king has commanded me to do something, and has said to me, ‘Let no one know anything about the business about which I send you, and what I have commanded you. I have sent the young men to a certain place.’
verses.arminianNotes: David claims to be on a secret errand for the king, which is untrue. Arminian readers see a real moral failure under pressure, the fear of man that Proverbs 29:25 calls "a snare," with consequences David will later own (22:22).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also call the lie what it is and do not excuse it. Scripture records the sins of its heroes honestly, and the narrative will show the cost of this deception falling on others.

verses.text: Now therefore what is under your hand? Please give me five loaves of bread in my hand, or whatever is available.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks for five loaves "or whatever is available." Arminian readers see real human need at the center of the scene, a hungry man and his companions, which Jesus later highlights when he cites this episode.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the one God has anointed (16:13) must beg for bread. They see God's provision coming through unexpected means, as he sustains David through the priest's help in his time of need.

verses.text: The priest answered David, and said, “I have no common bread, but there is holy bread; if only the young men have kept themselves from women.”
verses.arminianNotes: Only "holy bread" is available, given on condition that the men have kept themselves from women. Arminian readers note that Ahimelech applies the law with care, seeking to honor its purpose while meeting real need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the bread was set apart for the priests (Leviticus 24:9). Ahimelech's condition shows a concern for holiness, and the scene raises the question of how ceremonial law relates to human need.

verses.text: David answered the priest, and said to him, “Truly, women have been kept from us as usual these three days. When I came out, the vessels of the young men were holy, though it was only a common journey. How much more then today shall their vessels be holy?”
verses.arminianNotes: David insists his men are ceremonially clean. Arminian readers note that David speaks of "the young men," though he arrived alone, which may be part of his cover story; the text leaves this unresolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the uncertainty about whether men were waiting elsewhere. Whatever the details, the exchange shows both David and the priest treating holiness as something that matters.

verses.text: So the priest gave him holy bread; for there was no bread there but the show bread that was taken from before the LORD, to be replaced with hot bread in the day when it was taken away.
verses.arminianNotes: The priest gives the bread of the Presence that had been replaced with fresh loaves. Arminian and Reformed readers share Jesus' use of this event: "which was not lawful" for David, yet he was not condemned (Matthew 12:4).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jesus pairs this event with "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice" (Matthew 12:7). Both traditions see the ceremonial law serving God's merciful purposes rather than overriding them.

verses.text: Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD; and his name was Doeg the Edomite, the best of the herdsmen who belonged to Saul.
verses.arminianNotes: Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, is there "detained before the LORD." Arminian readers see the danger of David's deception: a hostile witness hears it all, and choices made in fear will have consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator introduces Doeg at the moment he matters most. WEB’s heading to Psalm 52 is, “For the Chief Musician. A contemplation by David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, “David has come to Ahimelech’s house.”” The psalm shows how David later reflected on this betrayal before God.

verses.text: David said to Ahimelech, “Isn’t there here under your hand spear or sword? For I haven’t brought my sword or my weapons with me, because the king’s business required haste.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks for a weapon, claiming the king's business required haste. Arminian readers note how one lie leads to another; David continues his cover story, making the deception harder to undo.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the anointed king has neither sword nor bread. God strips David of every human resource so that his eventual rise will clearly be God's work, not his own.

verses.text: The priest said, “Behold, the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the valley of Elah, is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you would like to take that, take it, for there is no other except that here.” David said, “There is none like that. Give it to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The only sword at Nob is Goliath's, kept "behind the ephod." David says, "There is none like that." Arminian readers see a reminder of God's past deliverance, calling David to trust the same God now.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the meaning of Goliath's sword returning to David's hand. The trophy of God's victory in the valley of Elah becomes a token of God's faithfulness to his anointed in a dark season.
